thr.no_lists: No threat lists loaded. Put one address or network per line in data/threats/<name>.txt and restart.
rec.title: Flow records
if.title: Interfaces
if.no_counters: This device sends no interface counters, so there is nothing to compare with. Add a line like snmp 10.0.0.1 public under Settings → Names to read them over SNMP.
if.ok: Consistent. The flow estimate differs from the device counter by {dev}, within the statistical error of sampling ({err}).
if.low: The flow estimate is {dev} lower than the device counter. Likely causes: {causes}.
if.high: The flow estimate is {dev} higher than the device counter. Likely causes: {causes}.
cause.loss: {p} of this device's export packets were lost on the way
cause.sampling: the sampling rate is not known yet
cause.unsampled_iface: not every interface carrying this traffic is sampled
cause.dup: the same traffic is counted on more than one interface
blk.title: Blocked sources
blk.sub: Datagrams from these are dropped on arrival: nothing is decoded, stored or alerted on
blk.done_firewall: {a} blocked — block it in your firewall too
blk.firewall: A blocked sender can change address, and a UDP source address can be forged, so this stops a known nuisance rather than an attacker. For that, allow only your own devices to the collector ports in your firewall.
blk.no_collector: There is no collector to block anything on.
src.title: Sources
src.sub: Is every device sending, can it be decoded, is the sampling rate right
src.names_sub: Optional. Name networks, devices, interfaces and hosts, one per line.
issue.silent: Nothing received for more than 2 minutes. Check the export destination on the device and that UDP is allowed through firewalls.
issue.waiting_sampling: Templates received but no sampling rate yet. {n} records are held and will be scaled when it arrives, not counted as 1:1. Devices usually resend it within a few minutes.
issue.assumed_unsampled: This device has not declared its sampling rate, so its flows count 1:1. If it samples, have it export its sampler options, or give the rate under Settings → Names, e.g. device {a} name sampling=1000. If it exports every packet, add unsampled to that line.
issue.loss: {p} of the export packets were lost on the way here (gaps in their sequence numbers). Totals are compensated; per-host detail cannot be. If “netstat -su” on this machine shows receive buffer errors rising, raise net.core.rmem_max; otherwise check the network path.
issue.no_template: Data is arriving but its template has not. It is held and decoded as soon as the template arrives.
issue.clock_skew: The device clock is off by {s}. Times were corrected to arrival time.
issue.decode_errors: Some datagrams could not be decoded. Check that the device sends to the right port and protocol.
empty.first: Nothing received yet. Send sFlow to UDP 6343, NetFlow to 2055 or IPFIX to 4739 on this machine.
err.db_memory: The database reached its memory limit and could not answer. Choose a shorter time range, or start traffic66 with a larger -memory.
err.db_busy: The database could not answer just now; the reason is in the traffic66 log. The page tries again in 30 seconds.

geo.title: Countries/Regions and networks database
geo.sub: Shows the country/region and network (AS) of each remote address
geo.none: No database yet, so countries/regions and networks show as Unknown. Upload one below.
geo.installed: Installed as {f}. It applies to new traffic from now on.
geo.where: Accepted: .mmdb files (DB-IP, MaxMind GeoLite2, IPinfo Lite; countries/regions, networks or both) and IP-to-ASN tables (.tsv or .tsv.gz). Your own files are used first; the built-in DB-IP Lite answers the rest. Traffic already stored keeps the country/region it was saved with.
src.names_help: Easiest: click any address on any page and choose “Name it”. You can also write one entry per line here, for example:
fd.none: Nothing was found in this time range.
fd.none_open: No open findings: nothing needs attention.
fd.learning: Learning what is normal until {t}. Connections between your hosts and uploads to new destinations are reported after that.
fd.note: Checked every 5 minutes. With sampled data (sFlow, sampled NetFlow) the numbers are what the samples show, and a small scan can go unseen.
fd.false_tip: This will not be reported again
fd.k.brute: {src} tried to log in to {dst} ({port}) again and again
fd.k.lateral: {src} opened {port} sessions to {n} hosts that never offered this service before
fd.k.exfil: {src} uploaded {bytes} to {dst}, a destination it had not used before
fd.k.threat_out: {src} connected to {dst}, which is on the threat list “{list}”
fd.k.threat_in: {src}, on the threat list “{list}”, connected to {dst}
logo.title: Logo
logo.sub: Shown on the sign-in page and at the top of the menu
logo.hint: PNG, SVG, JPEG, WebP or GIF, up to 1 MB. Recommended: 416 × 144 pixels (shown at 208 × 72, the width of the sidebar), PNG or SVG with a transparent background; other sizes are scaled to fit.
geo.role_fallback: Used where the others have no answer
geo.remove_confirm: Remove {f}? What it held then comes from the other databases and the built-in DB-IP Lite.
geo.updated: Updated. New traffic uses it from now on.
geo.update_failed: Could not download: {e}. Download the files yourself and upload them.
geo.free_sub: Download one and upload it here. DB-IP Lite is already built in.
geo.f_dbip: Countries/Regions and networks. No sign-up, updated monthly. Built in; “Update DB-IP Lite now” fetches the latest.
geo.f_maxmind: Countries/Regions and networks (GeoLite2-Country and GeoLite2-ASN). Needs a free MaxMind account.
geo.f_ipinfo: Countries/Regions and networks in one file (ipinfo_lite.mmdb). Needs a free IPinfo account.
geo.f_iptoasn: Networks with their country/region (ip2asn-combined.tsv.gz). No sign-up, updated hourly.
geo.map_sub: {n} countries/regions · darker means more traffic · click a country/region to filter
sb.title: Capture files
sb.sub: Analyse pcap files apart from the live data
sb.explain: Upload packet captures from Wireshark or tcpdump. Each goes into a database of its own: the live data, its numbers and findings are not touched. Analyse shows that one file on every page (overview, Top 66, findings, flow paths, map, flow records); switch files in the bar at the top. Delete removes a file and its data.
sb.confirm_all: Delete all capture files and their data?
sb.too_many: At most {n} files; delete one first
sb.limits: Up to {n} files, each at most {mb} MB.
sb.not_capture: {f} is not a capture file. Use .pcap or .pcapng as saved by Wireshark or tcpdump.
range.bad: The end must be after the start
cl.title: Delete old data
cl.what: Deletes flow records, the hourly and daily summaries, interface counters and findings from before the chosen time. Deleting all data also resets what the detection rules have learned. This cannot be undone.
cl.admin_only: Only the administrator can delete stored data.
cl.confirm_days: Delete all data older than {n} days? This cannot be undone.
cl.confirm_all: Delete ALL data: flow records, summaries, counters and findings?
cl.confirm_all2: Really delete everything? The pages will be empty until new flows arrive.
cl.if_sub: When one link's traffic must go
cl.if_what: Deletes the flow records that went in or out of the chosen interface, and its counter samples. The hourly and daily summaries record traffic by application, host and dimension, never by interface, so they keep their totals: a chart over a long range still counts this interface's share.
cl.if_both: A flow record names the interface it came in on and the one it went out by, so deleting this interface's records takes those flows out of the other interface's view as well — they are the same records.
cl.if_locked: Deleting data by interface needs a registered copy.
cl.if_estimating: Working out what this would remove…
cl.if_keep: {n} hourly summary rows keep their totals
cl.if_confirm: Delete all stored data of {i}? This cannot be undone.
cl.if_confirm_days: Delete the data of {i} older than {n} days? This cannot be undone.
cl.if_done: Deleted {n} flow records and {c} counter samples of {i}, freed {s}.
as.devices_sub: Click one for its ports and cabling
as.what_racks: Where the equipment stands: sites, cabinets, and what is in which unit. Everything here is written down, never discovered — so when it and the network disagree, the ledger still says what was meant to be there.
as.what_devices: What the equipment is and what it is cabled to: make, model, serial number, management address, and every port with the port at the other end of its cable.
as.what_ipam: Which networks exist and which address is whose. Shows how full a network is, suggests the next free addresses, and reports what does not add up.
as.locked: This needs a registered copy. Everything already written down stays, and becomes reachable again the moment a licence is installed.
as.hidden_hint: Only the administrator sees this record.
as.unplaced: In the rack, unit not recorded
as.conflicts_sub: Read from the ledger alone, so it is the same answer offline
as.paste_what: Run the command you already run and paste what it printed: show lldp neighbors, show cdp neighbors, show interface status, show ip arp, show mac address-table. Nothing is installed on the device and no community string or password is stored anywhere. Paste the ARP table before the MAC address table: together they say which port a host is plugged into.
as.csv_what: Export a kind, edit it, and import it again: the id column ties each row back to its record, so a file that came from here updates what it came from instead of doubling it. A file with no id column adds; references are by name.

nm.missing: Fill in the address and the name (and the index for an interface)
nm.bad_net: {a} is not a network such as 192.168.3.0/24

rg.hosts_sub_c: Inner ring: the busiest clients; outer ring: the servers each one uses
rg.svc_sub_v: Inner ring: the busiest services; outer ring: the servers offering each
rg.svc_sub_s: Inner ring: the busiest servers; outer ring: the services of each
geo.lines_hint: Set a country/region for your internal networks (Settings → Names, Network) to see lines from them to the countries/regions they talk to.
lic.free: Traffic analysis and detection keep working in full, and no data is deleted; the features that need registering are marked where they are.
lic.mark: Reports and diagrams carry an evaluation mark.
theme.label: Theme
issue.agent_drops: The device itself dropped {p} of its samples (it reports this in sFlow): its sFlow export is rate-limited. Totals are compensated; per-host detail cannot be. Sample less often (for example 1:2048 or 1:4096) or raise the device's sFlow rate limit.
if.set_default: Set as default (the pages open on it)
if.is_default: The default: the pages open on it
ov.if_sub: In and out as the interface sees it
if.peers: Peer interfaces (not sampled; only the traffic through the sampled interface)
if.peer_note: Peer interface: not sampled, only the traffic through the sampled interface of this device
src.dir_no: without flowDirection (61): sampled interface inferred from traffic
if.capture_only: Interface check compares flows with the interface counters of sFlow, NetFlow and IPFIX devices. Local capture on this machine's network card has no device interfaces or counters, so there is nothing to compare here.

acct.err_too_short: The new password needs at least 8 characters.

acct.err_bad_user: A user name cannot be empty or contain spaces or colons.
acct.err_fixed: This run's password was given at start and cannot be changed here.

acct.users_sub: Every user sees the same traffic; only the administrator manages users, deletes stored data and changes how the installation is set up
acct.err_user_limit: This installation may have {n} accounts. A licence raises the limit; everything else keeps working.
acct.confirm_del: Delete the user {u}? Their open browsers are signed out.
acct.ldap_dev: In development: signing in to traffic66 with your company's LDAP or Active Directory accounts.
login.hint: First sign-in: the user and password are on the console, printed when traffic66 started.
bill.title: 95th-percentile billing
bill.sub: What a carrier would charge for each interface
bill.empty: No interface counters in this period. The figure comes from the counters a device reports, not from sampled flow.
bill.gap_note: Five-minute buckets with no measurement are left out, not counted as zero. Counting them as zero would lower the figure. Coverage is how much of the period it rests on.
bill.how_note: Inbound and outbound are each sorted over the period, the top five per cent of the five-minute samples are discarded, and the highest left is charged — the greater of the two directions. Months are counted in this browser's time zone.
bill.retention: Interface rates are kept for {n} days.
lic.install_sub: Install the licence you were sent. Nothing is written until it has been checked.
lic.paste: Paste the contents of license.json here
bill.marked: Interfaces billed: {n}. Mark the circuits you pay for; the rest of what a device reports is not a bill.
bill.all_shown: No interface is marked as billed, so all of them are shown. Mark the circuits you pay a carrier for and this page becomes the bill.
mark.chip_hint: Not registered — see Sources to register.
mark.note_body: Every measurement, detection and page keeps working, and no data is deleted. What registering removes is this mark, which is also added to what you export, copy or print.
wait.templates: Not yet — waiting for the device's templates. NetFlow v9 and IPFIX describe their records in templates the device resends periodically; it usually takes up to about 15 minutes for the first one to arrive. {n} records are held until it does, and none are lost. Nothing to do.
wait.sampling: Not yet — waiting for the sampling rate. {n} records are held so they can be scaled when the device reports it, rather than counted as 1:1 and under-reported. It usually takes up to about 15 minutes. Nothing to do.
wait.settling: Not yet — the most recent minutes are still arriving. Exporters report a flow after it ends, so the last {n} minutes fill in as they come. Nothing to do.
fd.k.fastscan: {src} reached {n} hosts on {p} ports within one minute
fd.k.chain: {b} was reached on {port} and then reached {n} other hosts the same way
